conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. To help me understand how things have felt for you lately, I’d like to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays confidential between you, me, and the medical team that’s caring for you and your baby. We’ll go at your pace, and if anything feels too uncomfortable we can pause.

Before we start, do you have any questions about the process or about me?

If not, let’s begin.  
Thinking back over the past week: overall, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Hmm… yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband sends me those silly animal videos—but it’s definitely harder. It’s like the laugh doesn’t last as long or feel as bright as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, but it feels kind of forced—like I’ll chuckle at a silly thing my baby does, but the laughter fades fast and I don’t really feel it in my chest the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come help so I could grab a coffee alone—but they’re way smaller than before. Mostly I’m just going through the motions, hoping the “yay” feeling will show up, but it rarely does anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe my milk wasn’t “good enough” or I’d done something wrong during his nap routine. I know, rationally, that babies just have rough patches, but the thought still pops up that I should’ve figured it out better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Like, I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds weird when he’s napping, even though I just checked the monitor and he’s fine. The worry comes out of nowhere, but I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly—still, it keeps popping up a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick flash of “what if something bad happens?” when he’s sleeping in the bassinet. It’s short, maybe 30 seconds, and it’s gone once I peek in and see him breathing fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when he won’t settle and the laundry’s piled up, I feel this tightness in my chest and think, “How am I going to get through the rest of the day?” It passes once I check off one small task, but in the moment it feels overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do get sad once in a while, but it’s more that my mind keeps ticking through tomorrow’s to-do list while I’m lying there. Takes me maybe an extra 20 minutes to drift off—then I’m up every three hours with the baby anyway.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had moments—mostly in the evenings when the house is quiet and I’m feeding him for the third time that night. It’s like a wave of “ugh, is this my life now?” but it’s not constant; it comes and goes a few times over the week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times last week—once when I dropped a plate and it shattered, and another night when he wouldn’t latch. I just sat there with tears rolling, thinking I can’t even do the basics right now. It lasts maybe five or ten minutes, then I wipe my face and keep going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I get frustrated with myself sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds as though the joy of new motherhood is being clouded by frequent self-doubt, worry, and waves of sadness that come and go. You're working hard to stay positive, but laughter feels dimmer, excitement is muted, and ordinary tasks sometimes feel overwhelming. At night, when the house is quiet, brief tears or a sinking feeling can appear, even though you know rationally that babies have fussy days. Despite these struggles you have not had thoughts of harming yourself, and you continue to care devotedly for your baby; that resilience is important and worth building on.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and authenticity of laughter, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only rare, muted enjoyment that is "way smaller" than before, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame that intrudes despite rational awareness, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring, unprompted worries ('a few times a day') that intrude despite quick self-reassurance, aligning with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>She acknowledges some days she feels overwhelmed and describes physical anxiety and inability to see how she'll get through the day, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your EPDS total of 13 places you at the upper end of the moderate/high-possibility range, where further clinical assessment is advised. You describe <sym>markedly reduced pleasure</sym> and <sym>interest</sm> in daily activities, <sym>repeated self-critical thoughts</sym>, <sym>recurrent anxiety</sym> about the baby's well-being, and <sym>brief crying spells</sym> several times a week. These features overlap with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, though a full diagnostic interview is needed to confirm severity and rule out other conditions such as <med>generalized anxiety disorder</med>. Because your score is 13 and you denied suicidal ideation, immediate emergency intervention is not indicated, but timely follow-up is strongly recommended to prevent worsening mood or functioning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment this week with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist trained in postpartum mood and anxiety disorders
3. Consider evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or, if appropriate, <med>sertraline</med>, which is compatible with breastfeeding
4. Build 20-30 minutes of gentle outdoor activity (walk with stroller) and brief rest periods when support is available
5. Share this screening summary with a trusted partner, family member, or friend so they can help monitor your mood and assist with baby care
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep blocks, and any worrying thoughts to review at your next appointment; if thoughts of self-harm develop, seek urgent care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
- Diminished pleasure/interest (Q1–2)  
- Self-blame/guilt (Q3)  
- Recurrent unfounded worries and brief “what-if” fears (Q4–5)  
- Episodic feeling overwhelmed (Q6)  
- Intermittent sad/miserable mood with crying spells (Q8–9)  
- Mild sleep-onset delay attributed to racing thoughts (Q7)  

Pattern  
Mood symptoms are situational, transient (minutes–hours), with preserved capacity to self-soothe; however, they occur multiple times per week and interfere with enjoyment and coping.

Anxiety features  
Low-grade, persistent worry about infant well-being; no frank panic attacks.

Safety  
Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No suicidal ideation reported.

Screening significance  
Findings consistent with mild–moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; not at safety threshold. Recommend routine follow-up with obstetric provider and consideration of formal EPDS and/or referral to perinatal mental health for further evaluation.
